title: Effects of intercritical annealing time on microstructure, tensile properties, and cryogenic toughness of newly designed ultra-low C low Ni Medium-Mn steel
abstract: An ultra-low carbon and low nickel medium manganese heavy steel plates was fabricated by quenching and intercritical annealing process. The effect of annealing time on the tensile properties and impact toughness were studied in relation to the formation of reversed transformation. The results show that excellent mechanical properties with yield strength of 680 MPa, tensile strength of 871 MPa, total elongation of 38.2% and high impact energy of 187 J at −60 °C were obtained. The microstructure comprised of ultra-fine grained ferrite and retained austenite (RA) together with a small amount of martensite after intercritical annealing. Increasing the intercritical annealing time resulted in coarser matrix microstructures, larger and more voluminous retained austenite, but with notably reduced stability. Highly stable RA enhances the work hardening capacity of the steel via sustained deformation-induced transformation (TRIP effect), significantly contributing to the toughening of the multiphase system. In addition, Austenite stability, rather than large-angle grain boundaries and the amount of austenite transformation, is the primary factor determining the low-temperature toughness of medium manganese steel.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Developing methods that consistently improve yield strength and lower the ductile-brittle transition temperature (DBTT) is crucial for processing advanced heavy steel plates designed for cryogenic environments [ 1–4 ]. Ni-based steels, including 9% Ni [ 5 ] and, 5% Ni [ 6 ] by weight, have been extensively utilized as primary materials in the storage and transport of cryogenic substances [ 7–9 ]. However, an excessive amount of Ni can significantly raise the production costs of cryogenic materials and adversely affect their weldability [ 10 ].

Medium manganese steel, recognized for its promising applications in engineering, has garnered considerable interest from researchers in recent years, owing to its superior strength-toughness balance [ 11–14 ]. Medium manganese steel is characterized by its moderate manganese content (around 5-8 wt%), which provides the capability to tailor its microstructure and mechanical properties through the adjustment of additional alloying elements and heat treatment methods. Niikura and Morris [ 15 ] proposed an alloying strategy of substituting 5% Ni with 5% Mn. This approach led to the development of steel exhibiting enhanced cryogenic impact toughness, achieved through a multistage quenching heat treatment that significantly refined its microstructure. Many researchers [ 16 , 17 ] have noted that the inclusion of elements such as Al, Mn, and C is crucial for stabilizing the austenite phase, and that the addition of Si [ 18 , 19 ] is strategically used to prevent kappa carbide precipitation. Wang et al. [ 20 ] conducted a systematic study on the microstructural evolution and elemental distribution in low-carbon (0.003–0.4%) medium-Mn (3.5–9%) annealed steel post hot and cold rolling. They highlighted that Mn diffusion and partitioning, along with the reverse transformation of austenite during annealing, are pivotal in forming a multiphase submicron martensite-austenite (M-A) composite structure. Recent studies on Medium-Mn Steels, including Fe-5.8Mn–5Al-0.32C [ 21 ] and Fe–5Mn-0.1C–2Si [ 22 ], have shown a significant improvement in the balance between strength and toughness by managing the TRIP effect.

In medium Mn steels, the mechanical properties are primarily determined by the characteristics of the retained austenite, such as size, morphology, and chemical composition [ 23 , 24 ]. Therefore. appropriate properties can be achieved through careful design of the alloy composition and the heat treatment process. A notable enhancement in strength and ductility has been achieved in thin steel plates through cold rolling and annealing processes. However, to the best of our knowledge, the application of medium-Mn alloying in heavy plate steel has not yet been explored in existing literature. In the present study, an ultra-low carbon and low nickel medium manganese steel was design. The tensile properties and impact toughness of the heavy steel plate were studied in relation to the formation of reversed transformation austenite by tempering at diﬀerent time.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs:
The experimental steel was melted in a vacuum induction furnace and cast into a 50 kg ingot.  Table 1 
                          lists the chemical composition. After being homogenized at 1200 °C for 5 h, the ingots were forged into slabs with a thickness of 150 mm. The equilibrium phase diagram for the steel, presented in  Fig. 1 
                         (a), was generated using the Thermo-Calc software with the TCFE-9 database. The Ae 3  temperature (complete austenitization at thermodynamic equilibrium) was calculated to be 720 °C. As shown in  Fig. 1 (b), the carbon content in austenite progressively increases with temperature. At 590 °C, the carbon content in austenite peaks at 0.22% and subsequently decreases. In contrast, the manganese content decreases steadily with rising temperature until it stabilizes. Elements like carbon (C) and manganese (Mn) enhance the stability of austenite, significantly effecting the mechanical properties of steels. Consequently, these computational findings offer valuable guidance for optimizing the intercritical annealing process.

The austenite start transformation temperature (Ac 1 ) and finish transformation temperature (Ac 3 ) during the heating process of medium manganese steel are important parameters for determining the annealing process. Using the DIL 805A/D automatic dilatometer, the Ac 1  and Ac 3  temperatures of the experimental steel were measured to be 566 °C and 743 °C, respectively, as shown in  Fig. 2 
                         (a). It is noteworthy that the experimental steel exhibits a linear and slow rate of volumetric expansion in the heating temperature range of 566–680 °C. When the heating temperature exceeds 680 °C, the rate of expansion significantly increases, indicating a marked increase in the reverse transformation rate of austenite phase transformation in the experimental steel.

The Continuous Cooling Transformation (CCT) curves for the experimental steel are depicted in  Fig. 2 (b). The experimental steels experienced martensitic transformation across a broad cooling rate, ranging from 0.1 to 50 °C/s, which was attributed to the improved thermal stability of the supercooled austenite due to the enrichment of C and Mn element.

Fig. 3 
                          presents the TEM microstructures of the experimental steel subjected to various cooling rates. These microstructures are composed of lath martensite featuring a high density of dislocations with widths between 300 and 500 nm. It is important to note that the martensitic laths width remains relatively consistent, irrespective of the cooling rates applied. This lack of variation is due to the nature of the martensitic transformation, which does not necessitate atomic diffusion. Instead, atoms shift en masse in a coordinated fashion, restructuring the crystal lattice, propelled exclusively by the difference in chemical potential before and after the transformation. The aligned lath martensite manifests through a shear stress-induced slip mechanism that is comparatively low, leading to the creation of high-density dislocations.

sections.heading: Hot rolling and heat treatment
paragraphs:
The Slabs were reheated to 1200 °C for 2 h for complete austenitization, followed by air-cooling to the start rolling temperatures of 1150 °C and finishing rolling temperature of 1000 °C ( Fig. 4 
                         ). The slabs were rolled to plates of thickness 30 mm via 10 passes using a ∅450 mm rolling mill and finally, the specimens were water-quenched to the ambient temperature. The surface of 2 mm of the specimens was removed to avoid the negative effect of oxidized scale and then tensile samples according to GB T228-2002 standard with a gauge length of 40 mm and a diameter of 6 mm were cut along the longitudinal direction (LD). The tensile samples were subjected to deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) in liquid nitrogen for 15 min to eliminate most of the unstable austenite. Finally, an annealing process at 650 °C for 60 min, 90 min and 150 min was performed respectively for tensile samples with carbon partitioning from the martensite to austenite.

sections.heading: Tensile tests
paragraphs: The tensile test was conducted at a crosshead speed of 2 mm/min using a 100 kN Instron tensile machine. All specimens were tested until failure. During the tensile experiments, force and displacement plots were recorded, allowing for the acquisition of stress and strain data.

sections.heading: Impact toughness tests
paragraphs: Charpy V-notch impact specimens, measuring 10 mm × 10 mm × 55 mm, according to GB/T 229–2007, were prepared in alignment with the rolling direction and subjected to testing with an Instron drop weight impact tester at temperatures ranging from −60 °C to 20 °C. To investigate the effect of holding time, durations of 30 min and 90 min were employed. For each condition, three tests were conducted and the average of these values was computed to serve as the final data.

sections.heading: Microstructure analysis
paragraphs:
SEM observations were performed in a ZEISS Ultra 55. EBSD measurements were performed using a Zeiss Ultra Plus analytical field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM), which was equipped with channel 5 software from HKL Technology, operating at an acceleration voltage of 15 kV. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analyses were conducted using an FEI Tecnai G2F20S–TWIN microscope. The D/max 2400 X-ray diffractometer (XRD) was utilized to calculate the integrated intensities of the (200) α , (211) α , (200) γ , (220) γ , and (311) γ  diffraction peaks, which allowed for the quantitative measurement of the volume fraction of austenite according to Eq. sections.heading: Microstructure analysis
paragraphs:
Fig. 5 
                          illustrates the SEM microstructures of the experimental steel annealed at 650 °C for different durations.  Fig. 5 (a) displays the microstructure after annealing for 60 min, characterized by lath-like ferrite and morphologically diverse reverted austenite. Most of the reverted austenite appears in thin films, with a small amount presenting as fine blocks. The microstructure post a 90-min anneal ( Fig. 5 (b)), still comprising lath-like ferrite and various forms of reverted austenite, but with a noticeable increase in the quantity of reverted austenite and a higher proportion of blocky forms. As the annealing duration extends to 150 min ( Fig. 5 (c)), the microstructure primarily contains coarse blocky austenite, with a significant reduction in the amount of filmy austenite, and some lath-like ferrite is segmented by reverted austenite into blocky ferrite.

Fig. 6 
                          shows X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the experimental steel.As depicted in  Fig. 6 (a), the austenite diffraction peaks increase progressively with the extension of annealing time. Through calculations, it is determined that the volume fractions of austenite formed after annealing for 60, 90, and 150 min are 31.8%, 38.7%, and 46.1%, respectively ( Fig. 6 (b)).

Fig. 7 
                          presents the cooling transformation curves of the experimental steel after annealing at 650 °C for varying durations. The curves indicate that martensitic transformation occurs in the steel during the cooling process after annealing, which suggests that the annealed microstructure of the experimental steel at room temperature consists of reverted austenite, ferrite, and martensite. When the annealing duration is 60 min, the martensite start transformation temperature (Ms) is 140 °C. As the annealing time increases to 90 and 150 min, the Ms temperature rises to 165 °C and 220 °C, respectively. It is known that the martensitic transformation temperature from austenite is closely related to the content of carbon and manganese. Generally, the less carbon and manganese in austenite, the lower its stability. Thus, it can be seen that the reversed austenite formed after annealing the experimental steel for 150 min has the lowest stability.

Prolonging the annealing time increases the diffusion time for Mn atoms, promoting the continuous migration of the austenite interface into the ferrite and the gradual growth of reversed austenite grains. Extending the annealing time increases the growth rate of reversed austenite, which can exceed the rate of element enrichment. This results in a decreased average concentration of Mn in austenite. However, the reversed austenite maintains high thermal stability, with only a small portion transforming into martensite upon cooling. Furthermore, as the annealing time increases, the morphology of the reversed austenite transitions from fine film-like to coarse irregular blocks, and compared to film-like reversed austenite, the stability of coarse blocky austenite is lower, which is one of the reasons that the martensitic transformation temperature increases.

Fig. 8 
                          shows the EBSD images of the experimental steel. The red regions represent reversed austenite, the gray regions are ferrite, blue lines represent high-angle grain boundaries greater than 15°, and red lines represent low-angle grain boundaries less than 15°. Notably, different contrasts of Kikuchi bands are observed around reversed austenite and ferrite. Combined with the phase transformation curve mentioned earlier, this is due to the high dislocation density of martensite itself and the formation of a dislocation density difference with the surrounding phase, resulting in different contrasts of Kikuchi bands.

Fig. 8 (a) shows the microstructure of the experimental steel after annealing for 60 min, predominantly composed of lath-shaped ferrite, polymorphic reversed austenite, and a small amount of martensite, where the reversed austenite is mainly distributed at the original austenite boundaries and the original martensite lath colony boundaries. When the annealing time is extended to 90 min, as shown in  Fig. 8 (c), the number of reversed austenite and martensite in the microstructure increases, and the grain size of reversed austenite slightly grows with some reversed austenite merging into coarse grains. As the annealing time extends to 150 min, as illustrated in  Fig. 8 (e), the microstructure of ferrite is mainly irregular blocky, reversed austenite grain size is noticeably coarsened, and the number of martensite increases significantly. This is due to the continual increase in average grain size of reversed austenite, with an obvious reduction in C and Mn concentration, leading to a reduction in thermal stability. During the cooling process after annealing, some of the coarser blocky reversed austenite transforms into martensite due to insufficient thermal stability, resulting in an increased amount of martensite in the annealed microstructure.

(a, c, e) phase maps (red, black and gray regions denote to austenite, martensite and ferrite, respectively) and (b, d, f) grain boundary maps (red and blue lines denote to low-angle and high-angle grain boundary, respectively)

Fig. 8(b)–(d), and (f)  show the distribution of high and low-angle grain boundaries formed after annealing for 60, 90, and 150 min, respectively. It is observed that the ratio of high to low-angle grain boundaries does not significantly change with prolonged annealing time, and high-angle grain boundaries are still primarily concentrated at original austenite boundaries and original martensite lath colony boundaries, indicating that annealing time has little effect on the distribution of high and low-angle grain boundaries in the experimental steel.

Fig. 9 
                          shows the TEM morphologies of the experimental steel.  Fig. 9 (a) displays the microstructure after annealing for 60 min, consisting mainly of lath-shaped ferrite with a high dislocation density and thin film-like reversed austenite with an average width of approximately 120 nm, along with a small amount of granular reversed austenite. With the annealing time extended to 90 min ( Fig. 9 (b)), the dislocation density in the microstructure is significantly reduced or even disappears, reversed austenite markedly grows, primarily comprising thin film-like austenite with an average width of about 180 nm and irregular blocky reversed austenite with a diameter of about 250 nm. When the annealing time is prolonged to 150 min, as depicted in  Fig. 9 (c), the microstructure mainly consists of blocky ferrite and polymorphic reversed austenite, with the austenite primarily being blocky, granular, and film-like, and significant differences in grain size between them, to the extent that some blocky austenite merges with surrounding austenite into abnormally coarse grains. This is because sufficient annealing time promotes the full diffusion of Mn atoms into austenite, causing the austenite boundaries to continuously move toward the surrounding ferrite regions (i.e., growth of austenite), until merging with the surrounding austenite into coarse grains. Additionally, the extension of annealing time benefits the annihilation of dislocations through slip and climb mechanisms, resulting in a marked reduction or even disappearance of the number of dislocations in the experimental steel.

sections.heading: Tensile properties analysis
paragraphs:
Fig. 10 
                          shows the engineering stress-strain curves of the experimental steel after different annealing times, and the specific tensile properties are presented in  Table 2 
                         . It is apparent that as the annealing time increases from 60 min to 150 min, the tensile strength of the experimental steel gradually increases from 871 MPa to 980 MPa, while the yield strength and elongation decrease from 680 MPa to 38.2% to 623 MPa and 32.6%, respectively. This is because as the annealing time extends, the quantity of reversed austenite notably increases and the proportion of large-sized blocky austenite grows, leading to a reduced stability of the reversed austenite, which actively undergoes the TRIP effect during the initial stages of tensile deformation, thereby significantly enhancing the tensile strength. However, as strain continues to increase, the reversed austenite cannot sustain the TRIP effect, which causes a reduction in elongation. Concurrently, the extension of annealing time also causes the growth of ferrite grains and a decrease in dislocation density, leading to a reduced resistance to dislocation movement, and thus, a decrease in the yield strength of the experimental steel.

Fig. 10 (b) is a magnified view of the green-framed region from  Fig. 10 (a). It shows that the engineering stress-strain curve of the steel annealed for 60 min exhibits a “smooth” curve, and when the annealing time is extended to 90 and 150 min, “serrated” stress fluctuations appear during the uniform plastic deformation stage of the engineering stress-strain curve, which tend to smooth out with increasing strain. “Serrated” stress fluctuations are commonly seen in ferritic steels and high manganese TWIP steels, mainly caused by the interaction of movable dislocations and diffusing interstitial atoms [ 25 , 26 ].For medium manganese steels, “serrated” stress fluctuations are due to discontinuous TRIP effects, and austenite with different levels of stability is the fundamental reason for this phenomenon. Cai et al. [ 27 ] believe that the uneven distribution of Mn elements in austenite and critical ferrite, which segment blocky reversed austenite into film-like austenite of varying thicknesses, are the main reasons for the presence of austenite with different levels of stability. Clearly, this explanation does not apply to the experimental steel here. A significant body of research indicates that the stability of reversed austenite depends on the concentration of C and Mn elements [ 28 ], morphology [ 29 ], grain size [ 30 ], stress state, and the influence of adjacent phases [ 31 ]. For this experimental steel, as the annealing time increases, the morphology of reversed austenite gradually shifts from uniformity and similarity in size to diversification and differentiation in size, thus resulting in reversed austenite with varying levels of stability. Moreover, the volume expansion caused by the martensitic transformation of the larger-sized and less stable reversed austenite during the cooling process after annealing exerts pressure on the surrounding reversed austenite, creating local stress concentrations, which weakens the stability of the surrounding austenite, further exacerbating the heterogeneity of austenite stability.

It is noteworthy that the engineering stress-strain curves of the steel annealed for 60 and 90 min both exhibit continuous yielding characteristics, but the steel annealed for 150 min shows a pronounced yield-point drop, as shown in the magnified green-framed region in  Fig. 10 (b). This phenomenon is due to the significant amount of martensite that forms in the steel annealed for 150 min under room temperature conditions, leading to an increased initial dislocation density in the microstructure and a rapid accumulation of stress in the early stage of deformation. Upon reaching a critical stress, a large quantity of immovable dislocations suddenly releases, causing the stress to drop. Although the quantity of martensite in the microstructure gradually increases with the extension of annealing time, the quantity of martensite formed is relatively low, and it is not sufficient to compensate for the reduced yield strength caused by the coarsening of ferritic grains. Therefore, the yield strength of the experimental steel decreases gradually with the extension of annealing time. During the 60-min and 90-min annealing periods, the formation of minimal martensite does not produce enough dislocations to significantly affect the material. Concurrently, the predominant ferrite phase helps to distribute stress more evenly, resulting in a continuous yield behavior in the stress-strain curve.

Fig. 11 
                          shows the work hardening curves of experimental steel after different annealing times. As the figure illustrates, the work hardening curve can be divided into three stages: the first stage is characterized by a rapid decrease in work hardening rate, which is mainly caused by the preferential deformation of ferrite; the second stage shows an increase in work hardening rate, representing the initiation of the TRIP (Transformation-Induced Plasticity) effect in reversed austenite, generating a strengthening effect; the third stage is a slow decline, due to the softening effect of the ferrite matrix becoming the dominant factor again.

As shown in  Fig. 11 (a), with the extension of annealing time from 60 min to 150 min, the work hardening rate drops to 2200 MPa and 120 MPa in the first phase, respectively. This significant drop is due to the noticeable grain growth of ferrite and the substantial reduction in the internal dislocation density as annealing time increases, making it easier for deformation to occur at the beginning of straining, which leads to a marked softening effect and thus a large decrease in work hardening rate. In the second and third stages of the work hardening curve, the work hardening rate for annealing at 60 min initially shows a slight increase followed by a slow decline. However, when the annealing time is extended to 90 and 150 min, the work hardening rate exhibits significant fluctuations that smooth out with increased true strain. Comparing these with the engineering stress-strain curve reveals that the fluctuations on the work hardening curve correspond to the "serrated” fluctuations on the engineering stress-strain curve, indicating that the fluctuations in work hardening rate are caused by the discontinuous TRIP effect.

It is noteworthy that as the annealing time increases from 60 min to 150 min, the onset strain corresponding to the beginning of the second stage decreases from 0.02 to 0.007, as depicted in  Fig. 11 (b). This indirectly proves that the stability of reversed austenite diminishes with the extension of annealing time, requiring a smaller strain to induce the TRIP effect in reversed austenite. In addition, the maximum peak A of the work hardening rate for 150 min annealing is significantly greater than the maximum peak B for 90 min annealing, and the peak corresponding true strain also decreases from 0.07 to 0.04. This is because the volume fraction of austenite in the steel annealed for 150 min increases significantly with reduced stability, which leads to a concentrated occurrence of the TRIP effect in a smaller strain range in a large amount of reversed austenite, resulting in martensitic transformation strengthening and thereby significantly enhancing the work hardening ability. However, due to the rapid reduction in the amount of austenite, the TRIP effect cannot continue in the subsequent straining process, resulting in a decrease in elongation.

sections.heading: Impact toughness analysis
paragraphs:
Fig. 12 
                          depicts the variation of impact energy with test temperature for the experimental steel, and the specific impact properties are presented in  Table .3 
                         . From  Fig. 12 , it is evident that the impact energy of the steel annealed for 30 min decreases slowly with the reduction in test temperature, dropping from 250 J at 20 °C to 211 J at −20 °C, and even maintains a high value of 187 J at −60 °C. This indicates that the steel annealed for 30 min exhibits good low-temperature impact toughness. In contrast, the impact energy of the steel annealed for 90 min declines rapidly with decreasing test temperature, plummeting from 194 J at 20 °C to 90 J at −60 °C, demonstrating significantly lower low-temperature impact performance compared to the steel annealed for 30 min. Notably, as the test temperature decreases, the difference in impact energy between the steel annealed for 30 min and that annealed for 90 min shows a trend of gradual increase.

Research shown [ 32 ] that large-angle grain boundaries are the primary barriers against crack propagation, effectively enhancing the impact performance of steel. This is because the direction of crack propagation is closely related to the misorientation between adjacent grains. The greater the misorientation, the larger the deflection of the crack during propagation, requiring more energy to propagate and thus effectively improving the impact toughness of steels. Additionally, an increase in the proportion of large-angle grain boundaries can be seen as dividing the grains into multiple “smaller grains”, reducing the dislocation density within individual “grains” during deformation, thereby alleviating stress concentration and enhancing resistance to crack propagation. By analyzing  Fig. 8 (b), (d), and 8(f), it becomes evident that the ratio of low to high angle grain boundaries remains largely unaltered as the annealing duration is prolonged, suggesting that the impact properties of the experimental steel are influenced by factors other than the variation in grain boundary angles.

Reversed austenite, as an important phase in medium manganese steels, is a key factor determining strength and ductility, and it also has a significant impact on impact toughness. Hu et al. [ 33 ], found that the reversed austenite induces the TRIP effect during impact deformation, which can effectively inhibit crack propagation, increase the energy absorption of crack propagation, and thus enhance the impact toughness of medium manganese steels. Zou et al. [ 34 ], stating that the TRIP effect not only effectively alleviates local stress concentration and delays the nucleation of microcracks but also consumes a large amount of energy at the crack tip. Increasing the transformation amount of austenite during the impact process can effectively improve impact performance. In this study, to determine the volume fraction of austenite transformation in experimental steels with different annealing times during the impact fracture process, the austenite volume fractions before and after impact fracture at −60 °C were measured, as shown in  Fig. 13 
                         . Calculations show that the austenite volume fractions before and after impact in the steel annealed for 30 min are 24.8% and 13.2% respectively, with a transformation amount of 11.6%. For the steel annealed for 90 min, the austenite volume fractions are 32.2% and 14.5% respectively, with a high transformation amount of 17.7%. However, the higher austenite transformation amount did not improve the impact performance of the experimental steel. Hence, it is evident that the volume fraction of austenite transformation is also not the significant factor affecting impact performance.

Based on the microstructural characterization, it is known that the reverse transformation austenite in the steel annealed for a short period ( Fig. 14 
                         (a)) mainly appears as fine, thin films ( Fig. 14 (a)-Stage I). Due to their inherent shape, size, and the pressure from the surrounding bainitic ferrite, they exhibit good stability. Hence, a larger crack tip stress is required to induce the martensitic transformation in them ( Fig. 14 (a)-Stage II), and even some austenite with higher stability needs to undergo plastic deformation to transform into martensite, i.e., the strain-induced TRIP effect. Therefore, the TRIP effect produced in the steel annealed for a short period during the impact process can effectively alleviate the stress concentration at the crack tip, blunt the crack propagation, or even terminate the crack propagation ( Fig. 14 (a)-Stage III), thereby significantly improving the impact performance of the experimental steel. The reverse transformation austenite in the steel annealed for a long period ( Fig. 14 (b)) primarily presents as coarse blocks, leading to lower stability and easier transformation into martensite under low temperature and low strain conditions ( Fig. 14 (b)-Stage I). Additionally, the martensite formed during the cooling process exerts pressure on the surrounding reverse transformation austenite, creating local stress concentrations, further reducing the low-temperature stability of the reverse transformation austenite. Martensite, being hard and brittle, cannot deform synergistically with the surrounding ferrite and austenite during the impact deformation, and is prone to forming micropores at the martensite grain boundaries ( Fig. 14 (b)-Stage II), providing rapid pathways for crack propagation and becoming a hidden danger for the deterioration of impact toughness [ 35 , 36 ]. Therefore, in the low-temperature impact process of the steel annealed for a long period, a lower crack tip stress can induce the TRIP effect, significantly weakening the effect of alleviating stress concentration and greatly reducing the energy absorbed during the impact process. Even some austenite with extremely low stability may undergo martensitic transformation just under the influence of the crack tip stress field before the crack reaches, and then the crack rapidly propagates along the micropores at the martensite grain boundaries ( Fig. 14 (b)-Stage III). Simultaneously, the formation of thermally induced martensite at low temperatures also compresses the surrounding ferrite, increasing the dislocation density inside the ferrite and at its grain boundaries, thereby creating local stress concentrations, reducing the intergranular binding force, and worsening the impact performance of the experimental steel. In summary, the deterioration of the low-temperature impact performance of the steel annealed for a long period mainly originates from the reduced stability of the reverse transformation austenite and the formation of a large amount of martensite.

Fig. 15 
                          shows the impact fracture morphology of the experimental steel at −60 °C. As illustrated, the fracture mode of the steel annealed for 30 min ( Fig. 15 (a)) is a typical ductile fracture, with the impact fracture surface primarily composed of large and deep dimples. There are fine dimples distributed around the coarse dimples, and there are apparent tear ridges in the dimple fracture region. These characteristics of the impact fracture surface all indicate that the steel underwent intense ductile fracture behavior during the impact process, which effectively hindered crack propagation.

Fig. 15 (b) shows the impact fracture surface of the steel annealed for 90 min, which mainly consists of fine and shallow dimples. Additionally, a small number of quasi-cleavage planes formed by the rapid passage of cracks through the martensite boundaries are observed around the dimples. Because the fine dimples and quasi-cleavage planes offer little resistance to crack propagation, there are fewer deflections in the crack path, which cannot effectively reduce the crack propagation rate. As a result, there is a noticeable decrease in impact toughness.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
The heavy steel plates, designed with a balanced medium-Mn and low-Ni, ultra-low C composition, exhibits high yield strength and outstanding low-temperature toughness. The main results can be summarized as follows. 
                         
                            1) 
                            When the annealing time is extended from 60 min to 150 min, the content of martensite in the microstructure increases, and the volume fraction of reverted austenite rises from 31.8% to 46.1%. Moreover, these austenite grains transition from a uniform thin-film morphology to a variety of shapes and sizes. 
                         
                         
                            2) 
                            Increasing the annealing time from 60 to 150 min enhances the tensile strength of the experimental steel from 871 MPa to 980 MPa, and induces serrated fluctuations in the engineering stress-strain curve. These fluctuations result from the increased volume fraction and decreased stability of the reverted austenite, which promote the TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) effect, thus improving work hardening. The austenite with varied morphologies and sizes exhibits discontinuous TRIP effects during tensile deformation, leading to the observed serrated stress fluctuations. 
                         
                         
                            3) 
                            As the test temperature was lowered from 20 °C to −60 °C, the impact energy of the steel annealed for 30 min decreased slowly from 250 J to 187 J, while the impact energy of the steel annealed for 90 min dropped rapidly from 194 J to 90 J. The austenite stability of the steel annealed for 90 min was significantly reduced under low-temperature conditions, causing a transformation from strain-induced to stress-induced TRIP effect, which weakened the effect of alleviating stress concentration at crack tips and reduced the energy absorption during impact. Furthermore, the formation of a large amount of martensite created micropores, providing fast paths for crack propagation, which further deteriorated the impact toughness. 
                         
                         
                            4) 
                            Excellent mechanical properties with yield strength of 680 MPa, tensile strength of 871 MPa, total elongation of 38.2% and high impact energy of 187 J at −60 °C were obtained via a short intercritical annealing time. 
                         
                         
                            5) 
                            Austenite stability, as opposed to large-angle grain boundaries or the degree of austenite transformation, is the principal determinant of low-temperature toughness in medium manganese steel.
